extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, law, and theology; educated public and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A close critique and analysis of doctrines and practices by which ecclesiastical authorities (especially the Roman Church) claim spiritual and temporal power, and an exposition of principles concerning civil government, law, conscience, and sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of Good and Evil in a Commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Commonwealth the measure is the Law, which is the Will and Appetite of the State, not the private appetite of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions should be judged by public law rather than by individual passions; judging by private sentiment is 'vain' and 'pernicious' to the public state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawful Marriage Is Not Unchastity
rubrics_metrics.description: The lawful use of wives (marriage) is not repugnant to chastity or continence, and therefore is not a moral vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that marriage makes a man unfit for the altar are false if based on mistaken moral philosophy or ecclesiastical constitutions; clerical continence is a church constitution, not a natural moral law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins of Clerical Celibacy Are Institutional, Not Natural
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition of marriage for clergy arose from institutional designs (e.g., to secure ecclesiastical inheritance and spiritual pretences), not from pure moral/philosophical grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prohibitions by their historical and institutional motives rather than assuming they express universal natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not All Non-Popular Governments Are Tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: It is erroneous to call all commonwealths other than popular (democratic) 'tyranny'; names like 'tyrant' or 'king' carry historical and partisan connotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate form-of-government labels with moral condemnation; consider practical effects (e.g., whether government prevents perpetual war) rather than merely the label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws Require Force — Men, Not Words, Govern
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that 'not men, but Law governs' is false in practice: laws are enforced by men and arms, not by words or paper alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the material and coercive basis of law; disregarding the role of enforcement leads to dangerous errors and false expectations about obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Civil Power Over Conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending the power of civil law from regulating actions to regulating thoughts and consciences (by examination and inquisition) is an error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magistrates may inquire about a minister's willingness to teach certain doctrines when employing him, but cannot rightly force private men to accuse themselves of opinions when their actions are lawful; compelling belief is contrary to natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of Law Interpretation Resides with the Sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: A private man interpreting the law by his own spirit, without permission of the commonwealth, is in error; explanation of laws belongs to the power that makes them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptures and other texts become law only when made so by the commonwealth's authority; exercises like preaching may be regulated by civil authority when the state has jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscure Scholastic Language Is Deceptive
rubrics_metrics.description: The writings of the school-divines are often obscure, barbarous, or otherwise misused words that hide truth and make men think they possess it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer intelligible language; inability to translate scholastic Latin into modern tongues exposes its lack of intelligibility and its tendency to stop further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of True Philosophy by Ecclesiastical Authority Is Wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishing or silencing those who propose true doctrines (e.g., earth's motions) without competent examination is suppression and usurpation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth should be examined by competent judges; if teaching true philosophy incites civil disorder, silence/punishment should proceed by civil law and authority, not ecclesiastical usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cui Bono (Who Benefits) to Attribute Authorship or Motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Among presumptions, the benefit of an action most evidently declares the author; 'Cui Bono' is a rule to examine who profited from false doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the origin of doctrines or actions, ask who gains materially or politically; this helps identify authors and motives behind religious or political errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine that the Church Militant Is the Kingdom of God Serves Temporal Power
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching that the present Church on earth is the Kingdom of God was used to claim pastoral and civil governance, enabling popes to assert universal monarchy over Christendom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess doctrinal claims for their political consequences; doctrines that conflate spiritual and temporal authority may indicate an attempt to seize civil power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal Infallibility as a Mechanism of Obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Asserting that the Pope 'cannot err' in his public capacity creates a psychological and doctrinal basis for unquestioning obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims of infallibility critically as instruments to secure obedience rather than neutral theological propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Ecclesiastical Loyalties Undermine Civil Sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching that bishops derive authority not from God directly or their civil sovereigns but from the Pope introduces foreign dependence and can enable civil war against the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should check the source of clerical authority and resist doctrines that place local ministers under external foreign power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions of Clergy from Civil Law Are Harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Exempting clergy, monks, and friars from civil law and public charges creates a privileged class that avoids penalties and public burdens, fostering dependence on the Pope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support equality before civil law; exemptions that remove penalties or fiscal obligations undermine the state's capacity and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious Titles and Rituals Have Political Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving priests the name 'sacerdotes' (sacrificers) or making the Lord's Supper a sacrifice causes people to imagine sacerdotal powers analogous to ancient civil-religious authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that ecclesiastical nomenclature and sacramental theology carry political implications and may be used to legitimize temporal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacramentalization of Marriage Grants Clergy Judicial Power
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching that matrimony is a sacrament gives the clergy jurisdiction to judge the lawfulness of marriages and legitimacy of children, affecting succession and inheritance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate claims that sacralize civil institutions; sacralization may transfer civil rights (e.g., succession) into clerical hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical Celibacy as a Political Tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial of marriage to priests serves to secure papal power over kings by preventing dynastic succession through clerical lines and by creating dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine institutional rules (like celibacy) for their political ramifications and role in consolidating hierarchical control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auricular Confession as Intelligence-Gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Auricular (private) confession yields information about princes and great persons, giving clergy superior knowledge of state designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat institutional practices that collect private information with suspicion as potential mechanisms of political surveillance and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonization and Martyr-Declaration as Political Enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonizing saints and declaring martyrs fosters obstinacy against civil laws and can compel subjects to resist lawful sovereigns under ecclesiastical censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize cults and sanctifications as social-political levers that can mobilize obedience against civil authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacramental Doctrines (Transubstantiation, Penance, Absolution) Consolidate Power
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines that ascribe to priests the power to make Christ or to remit/retain sins serve to bind consciences and secure ecclesiastical authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze theological claims for their capacity to command obedience or manipulate individual conscience; such doctrines may function as instruments of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purgatory, Indulgences, and Works as Economic Instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of purgatory, justification by external works, and indulgences enrich the clergy materially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify theological justifications that create financial flows to ecclesiastical institutions and treat them as suspect when they align with enrichment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daemonology and Exorcism as Means of Awe
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices of demonology and exorcism keep people in fear and awe of ecclesiastical power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question uses of supernatural fear to maintain social order; such devices can be exploited to sustain authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholastic Metaphysics and Obscure Distinctions Hide Error
rubrics_metrics.description: The metaphysics, ethics, and politics of Aristotle taught in scholastic fashion, with frivolous distinctions and obscure terms, prevent detection of error and mislead the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clarity and intelligibility in doctrine; distrust elaborate technicalities used to mask power or ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of Power Depends on Virtues, Not Suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Power is preserved by the same virtues by which it is acquired: wisdom, humility, clearness of doctrine, and sincerity of conversation; not by suppression of science or obscure language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess rulers and institutions by their moral qualities and transparency rather than by their capacity to silence critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Protect Authority That Protects in Peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man is bound by nature, as much as in him lies, to protect in war the authority by which he is protected in peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic duty includes defense of the protecting authority; the right of self-preservation does not extend to destroying the protector whose strength ensures one's safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point When Subjects Become Obliged to a Conqueror
rubrics_metrics.description: A man becomes subject to a conqueror when he has liberty to submit and consents, either by express words or sufficient sign; practically when his means of life lie within the enemy's guards and garrisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical conditions (control of protection and subsistence) rather than abstract claims to determine when conquest creates binding obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission/Composition During Conquest Can Be Lawful
rubrics_metrics.description: When submission involves giving part of one's estate or contributing to the conqueror, it may be lawful and not equivalent to assisting the enemy; such compositions can be a reasonable means of survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate degrees and motives of submission; avoid moralizing about acts done under compulsion that aim to preserve life and property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Faculties' Contraries Can Be Reconciled by Education
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary faculties (e.g., judgment and fancy, eloquence and reason, courage and timorousness) are not impossible to reconcile; education and discipline can enable different faculties to operate in turn as required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate character and capacity by the possibility of disciplined alternation and cultivation, not by expecting all faculties simultaneously at all times.
